tasks.title: True or False
tasks.statement: Determine if each of the following statements is True or False. In the Summary Answersheet, tick the correct answer (TRUE / FALSE) for each statement. No justifications are necessary for this question.

parts.question: In a photograph of the clear sky on a Full Moon night with a sufficiently long exposure, the colour of the sky would appear blue as in daytime.
parts.reference: T. The colour of the clear sky during night is the same as during daytime, since the spectrum of sunlight reflected by the Moon is almost the same as the spectrum of sunlight. Only the intensity is lower.

parts.question: An astronomer at Bhubaneswar marks the position of the Sun on the sky at 05: 00 UT every day of the year. If the Earth's axis were perpendicular to its orbital plane, these positions would trace an arc of a great circle.
parts.reference: T. If the Earth’s axis were perpendicular to its orbital plane, the celestial equator will coincide with ecliptic and the Sun will remain along the celestial equator every day. However, as the Earth’s orbit is elliptical, the true sun would still lead or lag mean sun by a few minutes on different days of year.

parts.question: If the orbital period of a certain minor body around the Sun in the ecliptic plane is less than the orbital period of Uranus, then its orbit must necessarily be fully inside the orbit of Uranus.
parts.reference: F. The semi-major axis of the orbit of the body will be less than that of Uranus. However the minor body’s orbit may have a high eccentricity, in which case it may go outside that of Uranus.

parts.question: The centre of mass of the solar system is inside the Sun at all times.
parts.reference: F. The centre of mass of Sun-Jupiter pair is just outside the Sun. Thus, if all gas giants are on same side of the Sun, the centre of mass of Solar system is definitely outside the Sun.

parts.question: A photon is moving in free space. As the Universe expands, its momentum decreases.
parts.reference: T. For photons the wavelength increases when the Universe expands.

tasks.title: Gases on Titan
tasks.statement:
Gas particles in a planetary atmosphere have a wide distribution of speeds. If the r.m.s. (root mean square) thermal speed of particles of a particular gas exceeds 1/6 of the escape speed, then most of that gas will escape from the planet. What is the minimum atomic weight (relative atomic mass), A_min, of an ideal monatomic gas so that it remains in the atmosphere of Titan?
Given, mass of Titan M_T = 1.23 × 10^23 kg, radius of Titan R_T = 2575 km, surface temperature of Titan T_T = 93.7 K.

parts.question: Find the minimum atomic weight (relative atomic mass), A_min, of an ideal monatomic gas so that it remains in the atmosphere of Titan.
parts.reference: As the gas is monatomic, (3/2) k_B T_T ≈ (1/2) m_g v_rms^2 => v_rms ≈ sqrt(3 k_B N_A T_T / M_g). To remain in atmosphere, v_rms < v_esc / 6 => M_g > (54 k_B N_A T_T R_T) / (G M_T) > 13.2 g. Amin = 13.2. Answers between 13.0 and 13.4 are acceptable with full credit. Half mark for understanding that atomic mass has no units.

tasks.title: Early Universe
tasks.statement: Cosmological models indicate that radiation energy density, ρ_r, in the Universe is proportional to (1 + z)^4, and the matter energy density, ρ_m, is proportional to (1 + z)^3, where z is the redshift. The dimensionless density parameter, Ω, is given as Ω = ρ/ρ_c, where ρ_c is the critical energy density of the Universe. In the present Universe, the density parameters corresponding to radiation and matter, are Ω_r0 = 10^−4 and Ω_m0 = 0.3, respectively.

parts.question: Calculate the redshift, z_e, at which radiation and matter energy densities were equal.
parts.reference: ρ_r0 (1 + z_e)^4 = ρ_m0 (1 + z_e)^3 => 1 + z_e = ρ_m0 / ρ_r0 = 0.3 / 10^−4 = 3000 => z_e ≃ 3000. Only z_e = 2999 and z_e = 3000 are acceptable answers.

parts.question: Assuming that the radiation from the early Universe has a blackbody spectrum with a temperature of 2.732 K, estimate the temperature, T_e, of the radiation at redshift z_e.
Estimate the typical photon energy, E_ν (in eV), of the radiation as emitted at redshift z_e.
parts.reference: Wien’s law: λ_max = 0.002898 / T_e = 354 nm. E_ν = hc / λ_max = 3.5 eV. Alternatively E_ν = k_B T_e = 0.71 eV. Use of either Wien’s law or E = k_B T gets full credit. Answers with E_ν = 3 k_B T or E_ν = 2.7 k_B T also get full credit.

tasks.title: Shadows
tasks.statement:
An observer in the northern hemisphere noticed that the length of the shortest shadow of a 1.000 m vertical stick on a day was 1.732 m. On the same day, the length of the longest shadow of the same vertical stick was measured to be 5.671 m.
Find the latitude, φ, of the observer and declination of the Sun, δ_⊙, on that day. Assume the Sun to be a point source and ignore atmospheric refraction.

parts.question: Find the latitude, φ, of the observer and declination of the Sun, δ_⊙, on that day.
parts.reference: As the longest shadow is of finite length, the Sun is circumpolar. cot(90° - φ + δ) = 1.732 => φ - δ = 60°. cot(φ - 90° + δ) = 5.671 => φ + δ = 100°. Solving gives φ = 80° (1.396 rad) and δ = 20° (0.349 rad). Given high accuracy, only ±0.5° is allowed.

tasks.title: GMRT beam transit
tasks.statement:
Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT), one of the world's largest radio telescopes at metre wavelengths, is located in western India (latitude: 19° 6′ N, longitude: 74° 3′ E). GMRT consists of 30 dish antennas, each with a diameter of 45.0 m. A single dish of GMRT was held fixed with its axis pointing at a zenith angle of 39° 42′ along the northern meridian such that a radio point source would pass along a diameter of the beam, when it is transiting the meridian.
What is the duration T_transit for which this source would be within the FWHM (full width at half maximum) of the beam of a single GMRT dish observing at 200 MHz?
Hint: The FWHM size of the beam of a radio dish operating at a given frequency corresponds to the angular resolution of the dish. Assume uniform illumination.

parts.question: What is the duration T_transit for which this source would be within the FWHM of the beam of a single GMRT dish observing at 200 MHz?
parts.reference: Zenith angle z = 39.7° => altitude a = 50.3°. Declination δ = 90° - a + φ = 58.8°. FWHM beam size θ = 1.22 λ / D = 2.33°. T_transit = (θ × 3.99 min) / cos δ = 17.9 min. Use of 4 min per degree is acceptable. Missing cos δ gets a penalty of 2.0.

tasks.title: Cepheid Pulsations
tasks.statement: The star β-Doradus is a Cepheid variable star with a pulsation period of 9.84 days. We make a simplifying assumption that the star is brightest when it is most contracted (radius being R_1) and it is faintest when it is most expanded (radius being R_2). For simplicity, assume that the star maintains its spherical shape and behaves as a perfect black body at every instant during the entire cycle. The bolometric magnitude of the star varies from 3.46 to 4.08. From Doppler measurements, we know that during pulsation the stellar surface expands or contracts at an average radial speed of 12.8 km s^−1. Over the period of pulsation, the peak of thermal radiation (intrinsic) of the star varies from 531.0 nm to 649.1 nm.

parts.question: Find the ratio of radii of the star in its most contracted and most expanded states (R_1 / R_2).
Find the radii of the star (in metres) in its most contracted and most expanded states (R_1 and R_2).
Calculate the flux of the star, F_2, when it is in its most expanded state.
Find the distance to the star, D_star, in parsecs.
parts.reference: D_star = R_2 T_2^2 sqrt(σ / F_2) = 9.208 × 10^18 m = 298 pc. Acceptable range: 298 ± 2 pc.

tasks.title: Telescope optics
tasks.statement: In a particular ideal refracting telescope of focal ratio f/5, the focal length of the objective lens is 100 cm and that of the eyepiece is 1 cm.

parts.question: What is the angular magnification, m_0, of the telescope? What is the length of the telescope, L_0, i.e. the distance between its objective and eyepiece?
parts.reference: m_0 = f_o / f_e = 100 / 1 = 100. L_0 = f_o + f_e = 101 cm. Exact answer required for credit.

parts.question: A Barlow lens of focal length 1 cm is now introduced between the objective and the eyepiece to double the magnification. At what distance, d_B, from the prime focus must the Barlow lens be kept in order to obtain this desired double magnification?
parts.reference: m_B = 2 = v / u, v = 1 cm, d_B = u = v / 2 = 0.5 cm before the prime focus.

parts.question: What is the increase, ΔL, in the length of the telescope?

A telescope is now constructed with the same objective lens and a CCD detector placed at the prime focus (without any Barlow lens or eyepiece). The size of each pixel of the CCD detector is 10 µm. What will be the distance in pixels between the centroids of the images of the two stars, n_p, on the CCD, if they are 20'' apart on the sky?
parts.reference: Plate scale s = 1 / f_o = 0.206265 arcsec/µm. sp = 2.06 arcsec/pixel. n_p = 20'' / 2.06 = 9.7 (~10 pixels). Acceptable range: 9.5 to 10.5 pixels.

tasks.title: U-Band photometry
tasks.statement: A star has an apparent magnitude m_U = 15.0 in the U-band. The U-band filter is ideal, i.e., it has perfect (100%) transmission within the band and is completely opaque (0% transmission) outside the band. The filter is centered at 360 nm, and has a width of 80 nm. It is assumed that the star also has a flat energy spectrum with respect to frequency. The conversion between magnitude, m, in any band and flux density, f, of a star in Jansky (1 Jy = 1 × 10^−26 W Hz^−1 m^−2) is given by f = 3631 × 10^−0.4m Jy

parts.question: Approximately how many U-band photons, N_0, from this star will be incident normally on a 1 m^2 area at the top of the Earth's atmosphere every second?
What is the ratio, R, of number of photons received per second from the star to that received from the sky, when measured over a circular aperture of diameter 2''?
parts.reference: m_sky = 20.76 mag. Extinction is 50%. R = (0.5 φ_st1) / φ_sky = 0.5 × 10^(20.76 - 15)/2.5 ≃ 100. Accepted range: ±5.

parts.question: In practice, only 20% of U-band photons falling on the primary mirror are detected. How many photons, N_t, from the star are detected per second?

tasks.title: Mars Orbiter Mission
tasks.statement:
India's Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM) was launched using the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) on 5 November 2013. The dry mass of MOM (body + instruments) was 500 kg and it carried fuel of mass 852 kg. It was initially placed in an elliptical orbit around the Earth with perigee at a height of 264.1 km and apogee at a height of 23903.6 km, above the surface of the Earth. After raising the orbit six times, MOM was transferred to a trans-Mars injection orbit (Hohmann orbit).
The first such orbit-raising was performed by firing the engines for a very short time near the perigee. The engines were fired to change the orbit without changing the plane of the orbit and without changing its perigee. This gave a net impulse of 1.73 × 10^5 kg m s^−1 to the satellite. Ignore the change in mass due to burning of fuel.

parts.question: What is the height of the new apogee, h_a above the surface of the Earth, after this engine burn?
parts.reference: r_p = 6635 km, r_a = 30275 km. Initial v_p = 9.929 km s^−1. Total mass m = 1352 kg. Δv = 128.0 m s^−1. v_p' = 10.06 km s^−1. New apogee r_a' = 35380 km, h_a = 29009 km. Acceptable range: ±150 km.

parts.question: Find the eccentricity (e) of the new orbit after the burn and the new orbital period (P) of MOM in hours.
parts.reference: e = (r_a' - r_p') / (r_a' + r_p') = 0.683. Semi-major axis a' = 20933 km. Period P = 30136 s = 8.37 h. Acceptable ranges: e ±0.002, P ±0.1 h.

tasks.title: Gravitational Lensing Telescope
tasks.statement: Einstein's General Theory of Relativity predicts bending of light around massive bodies. For simplicity, we assume that the bending of light happens at a single point for each light ray, as shown in the figure. The angle of bending, θ_b, is given by θ_b = 2 R_sch / r, where R_sch is the Schwarzschild radius associated with that gravitational body. We call r, the distance of the incoming light ray from the parallel x-axis passing through the centre of the body, as the “impact parameter”. A massive body thus behaves somewhat like a focusing lens.

parts.question: Consider the possibility of our Sun as a gravitational lensing telescope. Calculate the shortest distance, f_min, from the centre of the Sun (in A. U.) at which the light rays can get focused.
Consider a small circular detector of radius a, kept at a distance f_min centered on the x-axis and perpendicular to it. Express the amplification factor, A_m, at the detector in terms of R_⊙ and a.
parts.reference: A_m = Φ / Φ_0 = (I_0 2π R_⊙ h) / (I_0 π a^2) = R_⊙ / a (using a ≃ 2h).

parts.question: Consider a spherical mass distribution, such as dark matter in a galaxy cluster, through which light rays can pass while undergoing gravitational bending. What should be the mass distribution, M(r), such that the gravitational lens behaves like an ideal optical convex lens?
parts.reference: For f_1 = f_2 for all r, r_1^2 / M(r_1) = r_2^2 / M(r_2). The required mass distribution is: M(r) ∝ r^2.

tasks.title: Gravitational Waves
tasks.statement: The first signal of gravitational waves was observed by two advanced LIGO detectors at Hanford and Livingston, USA in September 2015. One of these measurements (strain vs time in seconds) is shown in the accompanying figure. In this problem, we will interpret this signal in terms of a small test mass m orbiting around a large mass M (i.e., m ≪ M), by considering several models for the nature of the central mass.

parts.question: Consider the observed gravitational waves shown in the figure above. Estimate the time period, T_0, and hence calculate the frequency, f_0, of gravitational waves just before the epoch of merger.
parts.reference: T_0 ≈ 0.007 s (acceptable range: 0.003 to 0.011 s). Frequency f_0 ≈ 142.86 Hz (acceptable range: 333.33 to 90.91 Hz).

parts.question: If the central object were a main sequence star, write an expression for the maximum frequency of gravitational waves, f_MS, in terms of mass of the star in units of solar masses (M_MS / M_⊙) and α.
Using the above result, determine the appropriate value of α that will give the maximum possible frequency of gravitational waves, f_MS,max for any main sequence star. Evaluate this frequency.
parts.reference: Take α = 1.0 and lowest possible mass M_MS = 0.08 M_⊙. f_MS,max = 2.5 mHz.

parts.question: White dwarf (WD) stars have a maximum mass of 1.44 M_⊙ and obey the mass-radius relation R ∝ M^−1/3. The radius of a solar mass white dwarf is equal to 6000 km. Find the highest frequency of emitted gravitational waves, f_WD,max, if the test mass is orbiting a white dwarf.
parts.reference: f_WD,max = 0.359 Hz (evaluated using M_WD = 1.44 M_⊙).

parts.question: Neutron stars (NS) are a peculiar type of compact objects which have masses between 1 and 3 M_⊙ and radii in the range 10 – 15 km. Find the range of frequencies of emitted gravitational waves, f_NS,min and f_NS,max, if the test mass is orbiting a neutron star at a distance close to the neutron star radius.
parts.reference: f_NS,min = 1.996 kHz (for M = M_⊙, R = 15 km); f_NS,max = 6.352 kHz (for M = 3 M_⊙, R = 10 km).

parts.question: If the test mass is orbiting a black hole (BH), write the expression for the frequency of emitted gravitational waves, f_BH, in terms of mass of the black hole, M_BH, and the solar mass M_⊙.
parts.reference: f_BH = 4.396 kHz × (M_⊙ / M_BH).

parts.question: Based only on the time period (or frequency) of gravitational waves before the epoch of merger, determine whether the central object can be a main sequence star (MS), a white dwarf (WD), a neutron star (NS), or a black hole (BH). Tick the correct option in the Summary Answersheet. Estimate the mass of this object, M_obj, in units of M_⊙.
parts.reference: Black Hole. M_obj = 4396 / 142.86 M_⊙ ≈ 31 M_⊙ (any answer between 13 to 50 gets full credit).

tasks.title: AstroSat / Exoplanets
tasks.statement: Note: This task set contains both AstroSat (T12.1-T12.6 from exam page 5-6, noting original numbering collisions) and Exoplanet questions (T12.1-T12.13 from exam page 20-27). Here we map the exact questions sequentially as presented in the PDF.

parts.question: Some X-ray sources like Cas A have a prominent emission line at 0.01825 nm corresponding to a radioactive transition of ^44Ti. Suppose there exists a source which emits only one bright emission line corresponding to this transition. What should be the minimum relative velocity (v) of the source, which will make the observed peak of this line to get registered in a different energy band counter of LAXPC as compared to a source at rest?
parts.reference: From LAXPC specifications and Doppler shift calculation across energy band counters.

parts.question: Estimate the incident flux density from the source at 1 keV, 5 keV, 40 keV and 100 keV. Also estimate what will be the total count per unit bandwidth recorded by each of the instruments at these energies for an exposure time of 200 seconds.
parts.reference: Using F(E) = K E^−2/3 and instrument effective areas/efficiencies.

parts.question: For this source, calculate the maximum exposure time (t_S), without suffering from saturation, for the CCD of SXT.
parts.reference: Using SXT saturation level of 15000 (total counts).

parts.question: If the source became 3500 times brighter, calculate the expected counts per second in LAXPC counter 1, counter 8 as well as total counts across the entire energy range. If we observe for longer period, will the counter saturate due to any individual counter or due to the total count?
parts.reference: Calculated based on LAXPC counters and saturation levels (50000 in any one counter or 200000 total).

parts.question: Assume that the counts reported by CZTI due to random fluctuations in electronics are about 0.00014 counts per pixel per keV per second at all energy levels. What is minimum exposure time, t_c, needed for the source above to be detected in CZTI with SNR at least 3?
parts.reference: Noise = sqrt(counts), SNR = Signal / Noise ≥ 3.

parts.question: Let us consider the situation where the source shows variability in number flux, so that the factor K increases by 20%. AstroSat observed this source for 1 second before the change and 1 second after this change in brightness. Calculate the counts measured by SXT, LAXPC and CZTI in both observations. Which instrument is best suited to detect this change?
parts.reference: Direct evaluation of counts for each instrument before and after the 20% increase in K.
